# Source Map — MAC-010, IMF 2022 Article IV Full Report (Mexico)

## Document frame

- **Type**: IMF Country Report No. 22/334, *Mexico: 2022 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report*, November 2022. The package includes Press Release PR22/373, the staff report, and an Informational Annex. Discussions ended September 23, 2022; the staff report was completed October 18, 2022; the Executive Board considered it November 2, 2022; and the press release is dated November 4, 2022. (pp. 1–2)
- **Accounting/basis**: The selected indicators cite the World Bank, CONEVAL, INEGI, the National Council of Population, Banxico, SHCP, and IMF staff estimates. General-government data exclude state and local governments and include state-owned enterprises and public development banks. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators, source note and fn. 2) The contents list separate public-sector statements using the authorities’ presentation and GFSM 2014. (p. 7, Tables 2–3)
- **Attribution boundary**: The staff report was prepared by IMF staff for Executive Board consideration; the press release summarizes the Executive Board’s views. (pp. 1–3)

## Baseline macro conditions

- Real GDP growth: 4.8 percent in 2021, 2.1 percent projected in 2022, and 1.2 percent projected in 2023. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators, “Real GDP”)
- Period-average unemployment: 4.1 percent in 2021, 3.4 percent projected in 2022, and 3.7 percent projected in 2023. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators, “Unemployment rate, period average”)
- End-period consumer-price inflation: 7.4 percent in 2021, 8.5 percent projected in 2022, and 4.8 percent projected in 2023. Period-average inflation: 5.7, 8.0, and 6.3 percent, respectively. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators, “Consumer prices”)
- Headline inflation reached 8.7 percent by August 2022, up from about 3 percent at end-2020; core inflation reached 8.1 percent. Food inflation reached 14.1 percent in August and accounted for over 50 percent of the increase in headline inflation above target. (p. 9, ¶5)
- Overall fiscal balance: −3.8 percent of GDP in 2021, −3.8 percent projected in 2022, and −4.1 percent projected in 2023. Gross public-sector debt: 57.6, 56.2, and 57.7 percent of GDP, respectively. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators)
- Current-account balance: −0.4 percent of GDP in 2021 and −1.2 percent projected in both 2022 and 2023. Gross international reserves: US$207.7 billion, US$205.7 billion, and US$207.4 billion; equivalent to 3.9, 3.8, and 3.8 months of the following year’s imports of goods and services. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators)
- PEMEX reported EBITDA of more than US$23 billion in the first six months of 2022, more than double the same period a year earlier. (p. 12, ¶12 and fn. 4)
- The 2020 poverty headcount ratio was 43.9 percent, using CONEVAL’s multidimensional measure. (p. 4, Selected Economic Indicators and fn. 1)

## Policy status — operational, proposed, and recommended

- **Operational**: Banxico’s policy rate stood at 9.25 percent after initially using 25-basis-point increases, then 50- and 75-basis-point increases. It was about 6 percentage points above the U.S. Federal Reserve’s rate. Markets priced a terminal rate of about 10.5 percent in the first quarter of 2023. (p. 10, ¶6)
- **Operational**: Retail fuel-price stabilization lowered inflation by an estimated 2 percentage points in 2022 at an estimated budgetary cost of about 1.5 percent of GDP. (p. 19, ¶23)
- **Operational**: Several food producers and distributors entered a nonbinding agreement to stabilize prices for 24 items, initially for six months. The authorities also provided a temporary tariff reduction on certain foods. (p. 12, ¶11)
- **Proposed budget**: The 2023 draft budget targeted an increase in the overall deficit from 3.8 to 4.1 percent of GDP. Staff estimated that the 2023 fiscal stance would be about neutral. (p. 13, Box 1)
- **Current reserve level and proposed reform**: FEIP reserves had fallen below 0.1 percent of GDP. The authorities estimated that at least 0.3 percent of GDP would provide sufficient resources for a fiscal response. Amendments proposed as part of the 2023 budget would enable use of headroom against the government’s debt ceiling to bring reserves closer to that level. (p. 21, ¶29)
- **Staff recommendation**: Further policy-rate increases were warranted; staff expected a rate of at least 10 percent would be needed for inflation to return close to Banxico’s 3 percent target within the usual two years or so. Its risk-management approach entailed a real ex-ante policy rate peaking above 5 percent in 2023. (pp. 17–18, ¶¶19, 21)
- **Staff recommendation**: Move toward more market-based fuel pricing and reinvest at least part of the fiscal savings in targeted support for vulnerable households. (pp. 20–21, ¶29)
- **Executive Directors’ recommendation**: Gradually increase productive spending, financed by tax reforms, to improve human and physical capital. (p. 3, Executive Board Assessment)
- **Staff recommendation**: Fiscal-framework reforms could include a well-calibrated debt anchor, broader expenditure coverage in the structural spending rule, a medium-term fiscal strategy, tighter triggers for escape clauses, and a strengthened fiscal council. (p. 21, ¶29)
- **FSAP recommendations**: Enable effective consolidated supervision of all financial conglomerates and amend the 2014 Financial Groups law to make application mandatory; enhance Banxico’s Emergency Liquidity Assistance framework; strengthen bank-resolution tools and expand the resolution regime’s remit to financial holding companies; strengthen cybersecurity oversight; and introduce loan-to-value and debt-to-income requirements. (pp. 24–25, ¶¶37–38)
- **AML/CFT recommendation**: Ensure adequate, accurate, and timely beneficial-ownership information; pursue the authorities’ planned beneficial-ownership register; strengthen consolidated AML/CFT supervision, resources, enforcement, and sanctions; and monitor fintech and virtual-asset risks. (p. 25, ¶41)
- **Banxico plan**: Banxico had undertaken a plan to launch a central-bank digital currency, primarily to promote greater financial inclusion. (p. 25, ¶40)
- **Authorities’ position**: The authorities preferred to retain the fuel-price stabilization mechanism, citing the administration’s pledge that fuel prices would not rise in real terms above their November 2018 level and the mechanism’s legal basis. They were interested in fiscal-framework reforms that would allow fiscal savings and debt-issuance funding to be allocated to the stabilization fund. (pp. 21–22, ¶31)
- **Authorities’ position**: The authorities expected Mexico could benefit from nearshoring and said manufacturing might be less affected than services in a U.S. slowdown. (p. 15, ¶18)

## Risks and quantified scenarios

- The balance of near-term growth risks was tilted to the downside. Principal downside risks included higher global inflation, sharper tightening of global financial conditions, and sharper slowing in global or U.S. growth. (p. 14, ¶17)
- In the illustrative scenario, global oil and food prices rose by 10 and 50 percent relative to baseline. With a temporary dislocation of inflation expectations, Mexican output fell to more than 1 percent below baseline in the first half of 2023. Adding a 1 percent decline in domestic demand brought output to more than 2 percent below baseline at the trough. (p. 16, Box 2)
- In the short term, Mexican GDP has an elasticity greater than one with respect to U.S. GDP. (p. 14, ¶17)
- Without significant structural reforms, potential output growth per capita was projected to recover to only slightly above 1 percent after 2024. (p. 14, ¶16 and fn. 5)
- NPLs rose modestly from low levels during the pandemic and began declining in 2021. FSAP stress tests found strong banking-system resilience, although some smaller banks might need additional buffers under severe stress. (p. 23, ¶35)
- The total capital-adequacy ratio increased to over 19 percent from 16 percent before the pandemic. (p. 12, ¶10)
- PEMEX’s debt remained high, including debt to suppliers, and spreads on its external debt remained above those on Mexican government bonds and most oil-sector peers. (pp. 12–13, ¶12)

## Fiscal framework and legal/institutional constraints

- Mexico’s balanced-budget rule and constraints on debt issuance limit the scope for countercyclical fiscal policy. (p. 20, ¶29)
- FEIP replenishment is restricted under the fiscal framework. The framework does not permit debt issuance for non-capital spending, and balance-sheet transfers to FEIP are likely treated as expenditures requiring a pre-identified revenue source or offsetting spending cuts. (p. 21, fn. 8)
- Using 2020 data, the authorities estimated that the top 20 percent of the income distribution accounted for about 45 percent of fuel-excise-tax collection, while the bottom 20 percent accounted for 6 percent. The IMF staff stated that broad-based tax-rate reductions were therefore likely to yield disproportionately large gains to richer households. (p. 20, fn. 7)
- IMF staff described retail fuel-price stabilization as disproportionately benefiting higher-income households. (p. 19, ¶23)
- IMF staff said Mexico had made good progress in aligning its legal and regulatory framework with the FATF standard and recommended an increased focus on effectiveness. (p. 25, ¶41)
- The 2014 Financial Groups law allowed conglomerates to request authorization voluntarily to operate as a financial group; staff recommended amending it to make application mandatory for all such conglomerates. (p. 24, ¶37)

## Distributional and data notes

- The administration was projected to raise the minimum wage from 42 percent of the median formal-sector wage in 2018 to 59 percent in 2022. Real per-capita labor income had increased by about 5 percent year on year by mid-2022; staff said fiscal efforts, the higher minimum wage, and other labor-market measures may have contributed. (p. 19, ¶24)
- Staff estimated that the output gap was about −2½ percent in early 2021 and nearly closed by mid-2022. (p. 9, ¶4)
- Gross international reserves remained adequate at 125 percent of the IMF’s ARA metric. (p. 11, ¶8)

## Source role and contrary material

- **Role**: IMF staff appraisal accompanied by a press release summarizing Executive Board views; the 2022 FSAP was conducted in parallel. (pp. 1–3; p. 2, financial-sector discussion)
- **Authorities’ emphasis**: Mexico’s external buffers, flexible exchange rate, fiscal discipline, substantial remittances, and resurgent FDI had helped it through the pandemic and recent tightening period. (p. 23, ¶34) They also emphasized the benefits of fuel-price stabilization and support for historically underserved agricultural communities. (p. 20, ¶27)
- **Staff emphasis**: Fuel subsidies were largely untargeted and disproportionately benefited higher-income households; productivity growth was weak; further fiscal-framework, consolidated-supervision, and AML/CFT-effectiveness reforms were needed. (p. 19, ¶23; p. 21, ¶29; pp. 24–25, ¶¶37, 41; p. 26, ¶43)

## Limitations and items for stronger-model review

- The extract contains the annex titles and page references but not the annex text. Reopen Annex III for debt sustainability, Annex X for fiscal-framework details, and Annex XI for the full FSAP recommendations. (p. 7, contents)
- `5B.6` public-investment evidence is partial. Box 1 identifies increased funding for priority infrastructure projects but does not provide a detailed capital-expenditure composition. Reopen Box 1 and Annex X. (p. 13, Box 1; p. 7, Annex X listing)
- `5B.2`/`5B.5` governance evidence is limited to the structural-indicator chart and general staff discussion in the supplied extract. (pp. 8, ¶2; 26, ¶43 and chart)
- The extract is an IMF consultation package, not audited financial statements. Staff projections, Executive Board views, and authorities’ views should remain separately attributed. (pp. 1–3)

## REOPEN REQUESTS

- The draft’s statement that “no IMF data-quality caveat [was] flagged in cover material” cannot be verified from the absence of such a caveat in the supplied extract.
- The complete debt-sustainability, fiscal-framework, and FSAP details require the annex text, which is not included in the supplied extract. (p. 7, Annexes III, X, and XI listing)
